mkt-b1-campaign-brief-from-product.q: A marketer pastes a raw, messy product description and gets a brief where the audience section says '[ASSUMPTION] Likely mid-to-high income professionals aged 30-45.' What should the marketer do?
options: Confirm or correct it using real knowledge before treating it as the campaign foundation
Delete the assumption since it wasn't explicitly requested
Ignore it and move straight to ad angles
Ask the AI to remove all assumptions from future briefs
mkt-b1-campaign-brief-from-product.why: Flagged assumptions are the prompt's safeguard against incorrect guesses quietly becoming the base of the whole campaign — they must be checked, not ignored or blindly kept.

mkt-b1-campaign-brief-from-product.q: Why does this lesson's prompt instruct the model to state the campaign goal (e.g., awareness vs. sales) explicitly?
options: It's required for the AI to run at all
An awareness brief and a sales brief should read differently, and omitting the goal causes a generic default
It determines which AI model to use
It only affects the word count
mkt-b1-campaign-brief-from-product.why: Naming the goal up front changes what a good brief looks like; skipping it causes the model to default to a generic brand-awareness brief that may not match what's actually needed.

mkt-b1-campaign-brief-from-product.q: A marketer treats the first generated brief as the final version and sends it straight to the design team. What common mistake is this?
options: Correcting flagged assumptions too aggressively
Skipping the campaign goal field
Treating a first draft as final instead of correcting and filling it in
Pasting a polished description instead of raw notes
mkt-b1-campaign-brief-from-product.why: The lesson stresses that the output is a first draft to correct and fill in, not a finished document — sending it unreviewed skips the human verification step that makes it trustworthy.

mkt-b2-product-brief-to-20-ad-angles.q: Why does the prompt require 20 ad angles to be grouped into 5 named categories (pain-led, outcome-led, etc.) instead of just asking for '20 ad angles'?
options: Categories make the output easier to format into a spreadsheet
It's required to test on Meta and Google simultaneously
It reduces the word count of each angle
An unstructured request reliably produces near-duplicate angles reworded differently, not real variety
mkt-b2-product-brief-to-20-ad-angles.why: An open-ended '20 angles' request tends to return the same idea reworded twenty times; forcing five distinct psychological categories is what produces genuine strategic variety.

mkt-b2-product-brief-to-20-ad-angles.q: A marketer shortlists their top 6 angles, but all 6 come from the 'outcome/aspiration-led' category because those felt strongest. What's the problem?
options: It defeats the purpose of testing different psychological approaches to buying
The angles need a stronger hook length
Outcome-led angles are legally required in ad testing
Nothing — strongest angles should always be prioritized regardless of category
mkt-b2-product-brief-to-20-ad-angles.why: The lesson explicitly warns against shortlisting all favorites from one category, since that defeats testing genuinely different reasons to buy.

mkt-b2-product-brief-to-20-ad-angles.q: Why does the prompt ask for a one-sentence 'why this works' explanation per angle?
options: It's needed for SEO purposes
It makes weak or generic angles easy to spot, since a vague explanation could apply to any product
It replaces the need for a campaign brief
It's only needed for LinkedIn ads
mkt-b2-product-brief-to-20-ad-angles.why: If the psychological explanation behind an angle could apply to any product, the angle itself isn't specific enough to be worth testing.

mkt-b3-generate-improve-ad-variants.q: In the hook-variant testing prompt, why must the body copy and CTA stay identical across all 6 variants?
options: To save time writing
Because Meta doesn't allow varying body copy
So the test result can be attributed to the hook alone rather than multiple changed elements
It's a platform character limit issue
mkt-b3-generate-improve-ad-variants.why: Isolating one variable at a time is what makes a test result meaningful — if several elements change at once, a win or loss can't be attributed to anything specific.

mkt-b3-generate-improve-ad-variants.q: The model scores each hook 1-5 and gives one-sentence reasoning. A marketer skims only the numeric scores and ignores the reasoning. What's the risk?
options: The scores will be wrong
The AI will lower future scores
Nothing — the numeric score is sufficient on its own
They miss the actually useful feedback, which lives in the reasoning, not the number
mkt-b3-generate-improve-ad-variants.why: The one-sentence reasoning behind each score is where the genuinely useful critique lives; the number alone doesn't explain what to fix.

mkt-b3-generate-improve-ad-variants.q: Why does the workflow ask for a second critique-and-revise pass on the same weak variant rather than always generating a fresh batch?
options: A second targeted pass on a named weakness often improves more than starting over blind
Fresh batches are against platform policy
It's required to avoid AI hallucination
It reduces API costs only
mkt-b3-generate-improve-ad-variants.why: Fixing the specifically named problem in a weak variant tends to produce a bigger improvement than generating an entirely new batch and hoping one is better.

mkt-b4-landing-page-copy-that-converts.q: A landing page headline reads 'Welcome to ProjectFlow' after a visitor clicked an ad promising 'Stop losing billable hours to status update emails.' What guardrail did this violate?
options: The CTA must be a button, not a link
The headline must directly continue the ad's specific promise, not restate the brand generically
Headlines must always be under 10 words
Landing pages must include a testimonial
mkt-b4-landing-page-copy-that-converts.why: A generic brand-first headline breaks message match with the ad's specific promise, which reads as a bait-and-switch to the visitor and tanks conversion.

mkt-b4-landing-page-copy-that-converts.q: Why does the prompt require '[PLACEHOLDER]' instead of letting the model write a testimonial or stat for the proof section?
options: Placeholders load faster on the page
Inventing a stat or testimonial would be a false, publishable claim
It's a formatting requirement for Codex
Testimonials are not allowed in landing page copy
mkt-b4-landing-page-copy-that-converts.why: Letting the model invent a testimonial or statistic risks publishing a false claim; a placeholder protects against that until real proof exists.

mkt-b4-landing-page-copy-that-converts.q: Why does the workflow hand the finished copy to Codex to build an actual page instead of stopping at the copy document?
options: Codex writes better prose than Claude or ChatGPT
It's required for SEO indexing
It automatically fixes weak headlines
Seeing real layout catches structural problems like a CTA buried below the fold that copy alone can't reveal
mkt-b4-landing-page-copy-that-converts.why: Reviewing copy in isolation misses layout problems; seeing it assembled into an actual page reveals issues like a strong headline undercut by a buried CTA.

mkt-i1-email-sequence-from-core-offer.q: Why does the prompt assign each of the 5 emails one explicit job instead of letting the model decide?
options: Without explicit jobs, the model defaults to restating the full offer in every email, the most common sequence failure
It's required by email service providers
It guarantees higher open rates
It shortens each email automatically
mkt-i1-email-sequence-from-core-offer.why: Without an assigned job per email, the model's safest default is to restate the offer each time, which is exactly the failure mode this structure prevents.

mkt-i1-email-sequence-from-core-offer.q: Email 4 is supposed to create urgency, but the offer has no real deadline or limited spots. What should happen?
options: Invent a countdown timer to make the email persuasive
Skip inventing urgency and stick to what's real, since false scarcity damages trust and can create legal exposure
Delete email 4 entirely from every sequence
Ask the model to imply urgency without stating it
mkt-i1-email-sequence-from-core-offer.why: The prompt explicitly bans inventing fake scarcity because false urgency claims damage trust and, in some jurisdictions, create legal exposure.

mkt-i1-email-sequence-from-core-offer.q: A marketer notices Email 3 (Objection) gets fewer opens and considers cutting it from future sequences because it 'feels negative.' What does the lesson say?
options: Objection emails should always be cut if opens are mixed
Objection emails should only be sent to repeat customers
The objection email is usually the one that converts the most hesitant readers, so skipping it is a common mistake
Negative-feeling emails should be replaced with urgency emails
mkt-i1-email-sequence-from-core-offer.why: The lesson lists skipping the objection email as a common mistake, since it typically converts the most hesitant readers even if it feels like the harder email to send.

mkt-i2-monthly-social-content-calendar.q: Why does the prompt require the content-mix ratio (e.g., 40% value, 20% promotion) to be fixed before generating any posts?
options: It's required by every social platform's terms of service
Without a fixed ratio up front, the calendar drifts toward mostly promotional content under time pressure
It reduces the total number of posts needed
It guarantees viral reach
mkt-i2-monthly-social-content-calendar.why: Fixing the mix before generating content prevents the calendar from defaulting to mostly promotional posts, which is the easiest content to write under deadline pressure.

mkt-i2-monthly-social-content-calendar.q: The generated calendar ends with a summary table counting posts per content type. Why does this matter?
options: It self-checks the calendar against the stated ratio so a skewed mix is caught immediately, not after a month of underperformance
It's just a nice-to-have visual
It's required for scheduling software imports
It replaces the need for theme rotation
mkt-i2-monthly-social-content-calendar.why: The closing summary table forces a check against the intended ratio, catching a skewed calendar immediately rather than discovering it after a month of weak engagement.

mkt-i2-monthly-social-content-calendar.q: Why does the prompt instruct that no two promotional posts should sit within 3 days of each other?
options: Platforms penalize frequent promotional posts algorithmically
Clustering promotional posts undermines the value-first feel that keeps an audience from muting the account
It's a legal advertising requirement
It ensures equal posting across all platforms
mkt-i2-monthly-social-content-calendar.why: Spacing out promotional posts protects the value-first feel of the calendar, which is what keeps an audience engaged instead of tuning out.

mkt-i3-analyze-competitor-messaging.q: Why is Deep Research (Gemini or ChatGPT) specifically well suited to this competitor research task, compared to a normal chat reply?
options: It's faster at generating creative copy
It has a larger context window
It browses many sources over several minutes and cites them, turning claims about competitors into something checkable rather than guesses
It can browse competitor social media directly
mkt-i3-analyze-competitor-messaging.why: Deep Research's ability to browse many sources and cite them in the final report is what turns a claim about a competitor from a guess into something the marketer can actually verify.

mkt-i3-analyze-competitor-messaging.q: A marketer wants to use a claim from the research ('Competitor X focuses on enterprise clients') directly in a campaign brief. What should they do first?
options: Use it immediately since the report already cited it
Ask a different AI tool to double-check it
Rephrase it so it sounds less specific
Open the cited source themselves to confirm it's accurate and current before using it
mkt-i3-analyze-competitor-messaging.why: An unsourced claim used as-is is a guess dressed as fact; opening the cited source personally is what makes it trustworthy enough to build positioning on.

mkt-i3-analyze-competitor-messaging.q: Why does the prompt explicitly ask what competitors are NOT saying, not just what they claim?
options: It reframes research from 'copy what works' to 'find the open space,' which is more useful for real differentiation
It's a required field for Deep Research queries
It reduces the number of sources needed
Competitors' silence is always illegal to reference otherwise
mkt-i3-analyze-competitor-messaging.why: Asking what's missing from competitors' messaging surfaces genuine gaps to differentiate on, rather than just copying claims that are already saturated.

mkt-a1-repurpose-asset-into-ten-formats.q: Why does the prompt require each of the 10 repurposed pieces to be labeled with the specific source idea it's built around?
options: It's needed for copyright tracking
It prevents the classic failure of ten reformatted copies of the same paragraph by forcing variety at the idea level
It's required for scheduling tools
It shortens each piece automatically
mkt-a1-repurpose-asset-into-ten-formats.why: Labeling each piece with its anchor idea forces genuine variety at the idea level, not just the format level, avoiding the lazy repurposing trap of one idea stretched ten ways.

mkt-a1-repurpose-asset-into-ten-formats.q: A team publishes all 10 repurposed pieces on the same day to 'get it all out at once.' What's the risk noted in the lesson?
options: Nothing — simultaneous publishing maximizes reach
Platforms will flag duplicate content instantly
The pieces visibly compete for the same audience's attention instead of extending reach over time
It voids the original asset's copyright
mkt-a1-repurpose-asset-into-ten-formats.why: Posting all ten pieces at once cannibalizes reach across the same audience; scheduling them over 1-2 weeks extends the value of the source asset instead.

mkt-a1-repurpose-asset-into-ten-formats.q: Why does the lesson recommend reading the source asset yourself first, rather than letting the model find standout ideas unsupervised?
options: The model can't read long transcripts
It's faster to read manually than to prompt
It avoids copyright issues
Relying on the model unsupervised tends to surface generic points rather than the most distinctive ones
mkt-a1-repurpose-asset-into-ten-formats.why: A human pass over the source material tends to surface the genuinely distinctive ideas, while an unsupervised model pass tends to pick the safest, most generic points.

copy-b1-three-draft-directions.q: Why does the prompt require three genuinely different structural approaches (story-led, claim-led, question-led) rather than just asking for '3 versions'?
options: An unstructured request reliably produces three drafts with the same bones and different adjectives
It's a client billing requirement
It guarantees a higher word count
Only three structures exist in copywriting
copy-b1-three-draft-directions.why: Naming distinct structural approaches is what forces real divergence; an unstructured request for 'three versions' tends to produce three drafts that are structurally the same.

copy-b1-three-draft-directions.q: Why does the prompt ask for three complete drafts instead of three outlines?
options: Outlines take longer to write
Tone and rhythm problems, where most real copy decisions happen, only show up in actual prose
Clients never read outlines
Complete drafts are required for SEO
copy-b1-three-draft-directions.why: Outlines hide tone and rhythm problems that only surface in actual prose, which is where most real copy decisions get made.

copy-b1-three-draft-directions.q: A copywriter edits and polishes the first direction before reading all three. What's the issue?
options: It saves time overall
It's required to check grammar early
It anchors judgment on whichever direction was seen first, undermining the point of generating real options
Editing early always improves final quality
copy-b1-three-draft-directions.why: Editing the first direction before comparing all three anchors judgment on whatever was seen first, which defeats the purpose of generating genuinely distinct options.

copy-b2-edit-tighten-preserve-voice.q: Why does the editing prompt require pasting 2-3 real voice samples before asking for any cut?
options: It's needed to check for plagiarism
It shortens the editing time by half
Voice samples are required for copyright registration
It turns 'keep the voice' into a concrete pattern the model can match, instead of a vague instruction that leads to flattening
copy-b2-edit-tighten-preserve-voice.why: Real voice samples give the model a concrete target to pattern-match, which is the difference between an edit that sounds like the original writer and one that sounds like a competent stranger.

copy-b2-edit-tighten-preserve-voice.q: A client's distinctive, slightly irreverent blog intro is cut for length, and the edited version reads as generic corporate copy. What likely went wrong?
options: The edit tightened by flattening personality along with the fat, likely because no voice samples anchored the model
The target word count was set too low
The client's original voice was never good to begin with
The model refused to follow instructions
copy-b2-edit-tighten-preserve-voice.why: Without real voice samples anchoring the edit, the default AI tightening pass flattens personality along with the actual fat, producing generic-sounding prose.

copy-b2-edit-tighten-preserve-voice.q: Why does the prompt ask the editor to name the specific problem ('too long,' 'weak opening') instead of just saying 'make it better'?
options: Vague instructions are against platform policy
Naming the actual problem focuses the cut on what's genuinely wrong instead of random trimming
It's required to generate a word count estimate
It prevents the model from changing the CTA
copy-b2-edit-tighten-preserve-voice.why: Naming the specific problem focuses the edit on what's actually broken, rather than producing a generic tightening pass that cuts randomly.

copy-b3-headline-systems.q: Why does the headline prompt require 4 headlines from each of 5 named formulas rather than one open list of 20?
options: It matches a legal requirement for A/B testing
It reduces total generation time
Naming formulas up front produces structurally different headlines instead of the same idea reworded
Each formula corresponds to a different platform
copy-b3-headline-systems.why: Named formulas force structural variety; an open-ended '20 headlines' request most commonly produces minor rewordings of one or two ideas.

copy-b3-headline-systems.q: A copywriter shortlists all 3 finalists from the single highest-scoring formula category. What's wrong with this approach?
options: Nothing, highest score should always win
It violates the prompt's word limit
Scores can't be compared across formulas
It loses the point of testing genuinely different psychological approaches
copy-b3-headline-systems.why: The lesson recommends shortlisting from at least two different formulas, since picking all finalists from one category defeats testing different psychological approaches.

copy-b3-headline-systems.q: The prompt explicitly says not to invent a bigger stat than what's actually available. Why does this matter here?
options: Bigger stats always perform worse in tests
An invented, unsupported number in a headline is a claim the copywriter can't defend if challenged
It's a platform character-limit issue
It only applies to email subject lines
copy-b3-headline-systems.why: A headline built on an invented, more impressive number is a specific claim that can't be defended if a client or reader challenges it.

copy-i1-research-backed-copy.q: Why does this lesson separate research (ChatGPT Deep Research) from the drafting step instead of researching and writing in one pass?
options: It's faster overall
A drafting-only prompt under deadline pressure often invents a plausible-sounding but unsupported number because that completes the sentence best
ChatGPT cannot generate copy at all
Separating steps is required for SEO
copy-i1-research-backed-copy.why: Under deadline pressure, a combined research-and-draft pass tends to produce a confident but unsupported number because that's what best completes the sentence, not because it's verified true.

copy-i1-research-backed-copy.q: The research turns up a statistic from a source dated 3 years ago. What should happen next per the lesson?
options: Use it as-is since it's already sourced and cited
Flag it as potentially outdated since an accurate but old figure can still mislead readers about the current market
Double the number to account for growth
Remove all dates before using it in copy
copy-i1-research-backed-copy.why: A genuinely accurate but multi-year-old statistic can still mislead a reader into thinking it reflects the current market, so source age should be flagged.

copy-i1-research-backed-copy.q: No reliable source can be found for a claim the copywriter wanted to make. What's the recommended action?
options: Keep the specific number anyway since it sounds credible
Ask a different AI model until one confirms the number
Publish it with a disclaimer footnote
Cut the claim or replace it with softer, honest phrasing rather than keeping an unsupported number
copy-i1-research-backed-copy.why: When no solid source exists for a specific claim, the lesson recommends cutting it or softening the phrasing honestly rather than keeping an unverifiable number.

copy-i2-client-revision-rounds.q: A client's feedback includes 'make it more premium' and, later in the same email, 'keep it casual, our audience is relaxed.' What should the revision prompt do?
options: Flag the contradiction explicitly rather than silently resolving it
Silently pick 'casual' since it was mentioned last
Apply both changes by alternating paragraphs
Ignore both notes since they conflict
copy-i2-client-revision-rounds.why: The prompt requires listing contradictions explicitly instead of silently choosing one, which prevents the revision from resolving a note in a way the client didn't actually intend.

copy-i2-client-revision-rounds.q: Why does the prompt apply specific asks before vague directional notes?
options: Specific asks are always more important to the client
Vague notes translated first risk overriding a precise instruction buried in the same feedback
It's alphabetical order
Vague notes take longer to process
copy-i2-client-revision-rounds.why: Applying vague direction first risks overcorrecting in a way that buries or overrides a precise, unambiguous ask hidden in the same feedback.

copy-i2-client-revision-rounds.q: Why does the prompt require a change log mapping each feedback note to the specific change made?
options: It's required for invoicing clients by the hour
It automatically fixes contradictory notes
It makes the revision defensible — a client can see exactly which note produced which change
It replaces the need for a final human read-through
copy-i2-client-revision-rounds.why: The change log turns a vague disagreement ('this doesn't feel like what I asked for') into something specific and resolvable by showing exactly which note produced which change.

copy-a1-personal-style-guide-asset.q: Why does the prompt insist that every named trait ('conversational,' 'punchy') be backed by a specific, quotable mechanism?
options: It's required for trademark purposes
It shortens the style guide
Quoted examples are needed for legal citation
A vague adjective gives the model nothing concrete to pattern-match against, while a specific mechanism it can reliably apply
copy-a1-personal-style-guide-asset.why: 'Write conversationally' means almost nothing to a model, but a named, quoted mechanism like short declarative sentences is something it can reliably pattern-match against.

copy-a1-personal-style-guide-asset.q: Why does the lesson recommend building the style guide from a writer's 5-10 best, most distinctive samples rather than average or rushed ones?
options: Building from average writing captures less-distinctive patterns and produces a weaker, less useful guide
Best samples are always the longest
It's the only way to get the model to respond
Distinctive samples are required for copyright
copy-a1-personal-style-guide-asset.why: Rushed or average writing samples don't capture what's genuinely distinctive about a writer's voice, producing a weaker guide than one built from their best work.

copy-a1-personal-style-guide-asset.q: After building the guide, why does the lesson recommend immediately testing it on a new, unrelated piece of writing?
options: Testing is required before saving any prompt
An inaccurate or incomplete pattern in the guide goes uncaught if never tested against a real new draft
New pieces always score higher
It verifies the model isn't hallucinating facts
copy-a1-personal-style-guide-asset.why: Without testing the guide on a fresh draft, an inaccurate or incomplete pattern in the guide would go unnoticed and keep steering future drafts toward the wrong voice.
